The FOMC cut the federal funds rate 25 bp to 1.50–1.75% and initiated balance-sheet operations (T-bill purchases and repos) to maintain ample reserves, citing below-target inflation, solid household spending, and weak business investment/exports. In Svensson’s inflation-targeting framework, easing when inflation and market-based inflation compensation are below 2% appropriately supports expectations and price stability. Empirical VAR evidence (Sims, 1992) and DSGE transmission results (e.g., Christiano and Eichenbaum, 1992b) indicate that expansionary monetary shocks can lift real activity and labor demand, making this stance modestly growth-supportive near term. However, subdued investment and external weakness, along with still-muted inflation expectations (as in survey evidence highlighted by Bullard), underscore downside risks and possible labor-market hysteresis, justifying a cautious tone. Overall, the policy is moderately positive for the outlook but with meaningful uncertainty.
